auxiliary_material: The study design involved fully controlled feeding where all calorie-containing meals were provided, with weekly dietitian meetings for up to 10 weeks. Patients received various ICB regimens (pembrolizumab, nivolumab, ipilimumab+nivo, nivo+relatlimab) across adjuvant, neoadjuvant, and unresectable settings. The abstract explicitly states the primary objective was to establish effects on the gut microbiome, but this report focuses on cancer-specific outcomes. Limitations include small sample size (n=43 initiated), specific population (melanoma), and the artificial nature of fully controlled feeding which may limit generalizability to free-living populations.
outline_action: Cite this study as evidence that dietary intervention can improve ICI clinical outcomes in a randomized setting. remaining_gap: The success criterion requires confirming a causal chain where diet changes the microbiome which directly improves ICI efficacy. While this study confirms the 'Diet -> ICI Efficacy' link in a randomized trial, the supplied text does not report the microbiome data (structure or function changes) required to establish the 'Diet -> Microbiome' link or the mediation analysis. The abstract explicitly notes it reports exploratory clinical outcomes while the primary microbiome objective is not detailed here. Therefore, the mechanistic causal chain remains unverified based solely on this material.
useful_material: This study conducted a proof-of-principle randomized trial (NCT04645680) in melanoma patients receiving immune checkpoint blockade (ICB), comparing a fully controlled high-fiber diet intervention (HFDI, 30-50 g/d) against a healthy control diet (20 g/d). The authors reported exploratory clinical outcomes showing that in the combined neoadjuvant/unresectable cohort, median event-free survival (EFS) was significantly longer in the HFDI arm versus control (not reached vs 20 months, p = 0.03), and objective response rate (ORR) showed a favorable trend (77% vs 29%, p = 0.06). Any grade immune-related adverse events (IRAEs) were lower in the HFDI arm (71.4% vs 93.3%). This material provides direct evidence that a specific dietary pattern can be implemented via controlled feeding and is associated with improved clinical efficacy and toxicity profiles in an interventional setting.
